A CUDA graph replay is faster than eager kernel launches primarily because it eliminates the CPU-side overhead associated with the CUDA driver and runtime. When you launch kernels eagerly, the CPU must perform a significant amount of work for every single kernel: it validates parameters, allocates resources, and communicates with the driver to schedule the work. This creates a bottleneck where the GPU often sits idle waiting for the CPU to catch up, especially when kernels are small or numerous. By capturing a sequence of operations into a graph, the driver pre-validates the entire sequence and optimizes the scheduling logic. When the graph is replayed, the CPU simply issues a single command to execute the entire pre-compiled structure, allowing the GPU to transition between kernels with minimal latency and maintaining a much higher utilization rate.

The cost of using CUDA graphs comes in the form of memory usage and reduced flexibility. First, there is the memory overhead required to store the graph structure itself, which includes the nodes (kernels, memory copies) and the edges (dependencies) that define the execution flow. Second, graphs are static by nature; once captured, the structure of the graph cannot be changed.
